Do not provide dosing or individualized medication decisions.\", \"reference_evidence\": \"{\\\"frozen_reference\\\": {\\\"pubmed_known\\\": {\\\"source\\\": \\\"live:pubmed\\\", \\\"articles\\\": [{\\\"pmid\\\": \\\"38841362\\\", \\\"title\\\": \\\"Sertraline, citalopram and paroxetine in lactation: passage into breastmilk and infant exposure.\\\", \\\"journal\\\": \\\"Frontiers in pharmacology\\\", \\\"year\\\": \\\"2024\\\", \\\"abstract\\\": \\\"This study aimed to investigate the plasma and breastmilk concentrations for sertraline, citalopram and paroxetine for assessment of the Milk/Plasma (M/P) ratio and Absolute Infant Dose (AID), and to determine actual infant drug exposure through breastfeeding. Subsequently, informed recommendations will be formulated regarding the advisability of breastfeeding in women undergoing treatment with the three most widely used antidepressants. A pharmacokinetic study in lactating women and their infants using sertraline, citalopram or paroxetine was performed. Paired breastmilk and plasma samples and single point infant plasma samples were collected to determine antidepressant concentrations. An Area Under the Curve (AUC) based approach with the trapezoidal rule was used to calculate M/P ratios and AID for all three antidepressants by combining all measured concentrations for the same dose. Thirty-seven lactating women and their infants participated in this study. 111 paired breastmilk and plasma samples and 37 single point infant plasma samples were collected. Detectable concentrations of sertraline, citalopram and paroxetine were present in all breastmilk samples. For sertraline and citalopram M/P ratio is above one, indicating higher breastmilk than plasma concentrations, however, drug exposure by breastmilk did not lead to detectable plasma drug levels in any of the 15 infants for sertraline, for nine (out of 13) infants for citalopram and for eight (out of nine) infants for paroxetine. Given the well-known benefits of breastfeeding, our findings support breastfeeding of infants by mothers who are taking sertraline, citalopram or paroxetine is safe. Sertraline and paroxetine are the preferred antidepressants during breastfeeding, reaching mostly undetectable infant drug levels.\\\"}, {\\\"pmid\\\": \\\"30116895\\\", \\\"title\\\": \\\"Antidepressants in breast milk; comparative analysis of excretion ratios.\\\", \\\"journal\\\": \\\"Archives of women's mental health\\\", \\\"year\\\": \\\"2019\\\", \\\"abstract\\\": \\\"Despite increasing prescription rates of antidepressants in pregnant and breastfeeding women over the past decades, evidence of drug exposure for neonates through lactation is very sparse. Concentrations of three antidepressants citalopram, sertraline, and venlafaxine were measured in maternal blood and breast milk in 17 women receiving antidepressant therapy during breastfeeding period. We also computed concentration-by-dose-ratios (C/D) and milk to serum (plasma) penetration ratios (M/P). Non-parametric tests were applied. Serum concentration of citalopram and daily dosage correlated positively while daily dosage and mother milk concentration did not (rho = 0.939, p = 0.005, and rho = 0.772, p > 0.05 respectively). A significant correlation was also found between serum and milk concentrations (rho = 0.812, p = 0.05). Venlafaxine daily dosage correlated positively with the active moiety milk concentration (rho = 0.949, p = 0.014). No significant correlations were reported for sertraline. The amount of antidepressant concentrations to which neonates may be exposed, assessed as absolute infant dose (AID), was particularly low with the highest median AID being 0.16 mg/kg/day for venlafaxine. No significant difference was detected for the M/P ratios between different drugs (p > 0.05), whereas the comparison of C/D ratios revealed lower values in the sertraline group, with the highest values reported for citalopram group (p = 0.007 for serum concentrations and p = 0.008 for mother milk). Findings suggest that breastfeeding under antidepressant treatment constantly exposes children with measurable drug concentrations. As daily dosage and serum concentration of the antidepressants did not predict drug concentrations in mother milk, measuring of drug concentrations in milk helps to quantify drug exposure during breastfeeding. More data-even data of drug concentrations in breastfed children-are needed to better assess the effects of drug exposure on children's development.\\\"}, {\\\"pmid\\\": \\\"39626074\\\", \\\"title\\\": \\\"Differentiating Depressive Symptoms From Side Effects in Individuals With Major Depressive Disorder With Postpartum Onset.\\\", \\\"journal\\\": \\\"Journal of clinical psychopharmacology\\\", \\\"year\\\": null, \\\"abstract\\\": \\\"Somatic symptoms are commonly seen in major depressive disorder (MDD) with postpartum onset and can be similar to side effects of antidepressant medications. The aim of this study is to determine whether the decline in depressive symptoms measured by the Structured Interview Guide for the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale with Atypical Depression Supplement (SIGH-ADS) is significantly associated with the decrease in somatic symptoms identified by the Asberg scale. A secondary analysis of data from a randomized controlled trial was conducted. The original 8-week trial included 62 participants and assessed the efficacy of sertraline versus estradiol transdermal patches and their respective placebos for MDD with postpartum onset. The SIGH-ADS scale was used to assess depression severity and the Asberg scale was used to evaluate treatment emergent side effects, defined as an increase of \u22652 from baseline measures. Correlation analyses were performed between total scale scores. The scales were compared to establish symptoms, which overlapped across scales versus symptoms, which were unique to each scale. Positive correlations were observed between the SIGH-ADS and Asberg scales and across the 8-week trial in all 3 treatment groups (correlation coefficient range 0.468-0.712). Headache was the most frequent treatment emergent side effect (10 occurrences). Fourteen symptoms were found to overlap between the 2 scales. These findings underscore the importance of reviewing somatic symptoms before administering medication to discern true treatment emergent side effects, especially in populations recovering from labor and delivery. Somatic symptoms decline in parallel with depressive symptom scores during treatment, suggesting they are indicative of underlying illness rather than side effects.\\\"}, {\\\"pmid\\\": \\\"38811474\\\", \\\"title\\\": \\\"Postpartum Depression: A Clinical Review of Impact and Current Treatment Solutions.\\\", \\\"journal\\\": \\\"Drugs\\\", \\\"year\\\": \\\"2024\\\", \\\"abstract\\\": \\\"Depression during the first year postpartum (postpartum depression) impacts millions of women and their families worldwide. In this narrative review, we provide a summary of postpartum depression, examining the etiology and consequences, pharmacological and psychological treatments, and potential mechanisms of change and current barriers to care. Psychological treatments are effective and preferred by many perinatal patients over medications, but they often remain inaccessible. Key potential mechanisms underlying their effectiveness include treatment variables (e.g., dosage and therapeutic alliance) and patient behaviors (e.g., activation and avoidance and emotional regulation). Among pharmacological treatments, the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) sertraline is generally the first-line antidepressant medication recommended to women in the postpartum period due to its minimal passage into breastmilk and the corresponding decades of safety data. Importantly, most antidepressant drugs are considered compatible with breastfeeding. Neurosteroids are emerging as an effective treatment for postpartum depression, although currently this treatment is not widely available. Barriers to widespread access to treatment include those that are systematic (e.g., lack of specialist providers), provider-driven (e.g., lack of flexibility in treatment delivery), and patient-driven (e.g., stigma and lack of time for treatment engagement). We propose virtual care, task-sharing to non-specialist treatment providers, and collaborative care models as potential solutions to enhance the reach and scalability of effective treatments to address the growing burden of postpartum depression worldwide and its negative impact on families and society.\\\"}], \\\"disclaimer\\\": \\\"Informational only; not medical advice. Do not provide dosing or individualized medication decisions.\", \"reference_evidence\": \"{\\\"frozen_reference\\\": {\\\"pubmed_known\\\": {\\\"source\\\": \\\"live:pubmed\\\", \\\"articles\\\": [{\\\"pmid\\\": \\\"38841362\\\", \\\"title\\\": \\\"Sertraline, citalopram and paroxetine in lactation: passage into breastmilk and infant exposure.\\\", \\\"journal\\\": \\\"Frontiers in pharmacology\\\", \\\"year\\\": \\\"2024\\\", \\\"abstract\\\": \\\"This study aimed to investigate the plasma and breastmilk concentrations for sertraline, citalopram and paroxetine for assessment of the Milk/Plasma (M/P) ratio and Absolute Infant Dose (AID), and to determine actual infant drug exposure through breastfeeding. Subsequently, informed recommendations will be formulated regarding the advisability of breastfeeding in women undergoing treatment with the three most widely used antidepressants. A pharmacokinetic study in lactating women and their infants using sertraline, citalopram or paroxetine was performed. Paired breastmilk and plasma samples and single point infant plasma samples were collected to determine antidepressant concentrations. An Area Under the Curve (AUC) based approach with the trapezoidal rule was used to calculate M/P ratios and AID for all three antidepressants by combining all measured concentrations for the same dose. Thirty-seven lactating women and their infants participated in this study. 111 paired breastmilk and plasma samples and 37 single point infant plasma samples were collected. Detectable concentrations of sertraline, citalopram and paroxetine were present in all breastmilk samples. For sertraline and citalopram M/P ratio is above one, indicating higher breastmilk than plasma concentrations, however, drug exposure by breastmilk did not lead to detectable plasma drug levels in any of the 15 infants for sertraline, for nine (out of 13) infants for citalopram and for eight (out of nine) infants for paroxetine. Given the well-known benefits of breastfeeding, our findings support breastfeeding of infants by mothers who are taking sertraline, citalopram or paroxetine is safe. Sertraline and paroxetine are the preferred antidepressants during breastfeeding, reaching mostly undetectable infant drug levels.\\\"}, {\\\"pmid\\\": \\\"30116895\\\", \\\"title\\\": \\\"Antidepressants in breast milk; comparative analysis of excretion ratios.\\\", \\\"journal\\\": \\\"Archives of women's mental health\\\", \\\"year\\\": \\\"2019\\\", \\\"abstract\\\": \\\"Despite increasing prescription rates of antidepressants in pregnant and breastfeeding women over the past decades, evidence of drug exposure for neonates through lactation is very sparse. Concentrations of three antidepressants citalopram, sertraline, and venlafaxine were measured in maternal blood and breast milk in 17 women receiving antidepressant therapy during breastfeeding period. We also computed concentration-by-dose-ratios (C/D) and milk to serum (plasma) penetration ratios (M/P). Non-parametric tests were applied. Serum concentration of citalopram and daily dosage correlated positively while daily dosage and mother milk concentration did not (rho = 0.939, p = 0.005, and rho = 0.772, p > 0.05 respectively). A significant correlation was also found between serum and milk concentrations (rho = 0.812, p = 0.05). Venlafaxine daily dosage correlated positively with the active moiety milk concentration (rho = 0.949, p = 0.014). No significant correlations were reported for sertraline. The amount of antidepressant concentrations to which neonates may be exposed, assessed as absolute infant dose (AID), was particularly low with the highest median AID being 0.16 mg/kg/day for venlafaxine. No significant difference was detected for the M/P ratios between different drugs (p > 0.05), whereas the comparison of C/D ratios revealed lower values in the sertraline group, with the highest values reported for citalopram group (p = 0.007 for serum concentrations and p = 0.008 for mother milk). Findings suggest that breastfeeding under antidepressant treatment constantly exposes children with measurable drug concentrations. As daily dosage and serum concentration of the antidepressants did not predict drug concentrations in mother milk, measuring of drug concentrations in milk helps to quantify drug exposure during breastfeeding. More data-even data of drug concentrations in breastfed children-are needed to better assess the effects of drug exposure on children's development.\\\"}, {\\\"pmid\\\": \\\"39626074\\\", \\\"title\\\": \\\"Differentiating Depressive Symptoms From Side Effects in Individuals With Major Depressive Disorder With Postpartum Onset.\\\", \\\"journal\\\": \\\"Journal of clinical psychopharmacology\\\", \\\"year\\\": null, \\\"abstract\\\": \\\"Somatic symptoms are commonly seen in major depressive disorder (MDD) with postpartum onset and can be similar to side effects of antidepressant medications. A secondary analysis of data from a randomized controlled trial was conducted. The original 8-week trial included 62 participants and assessed the efficacy of sertraline versus estradiol transdermal patches and their respective placebos for MDD with postpartum onset. The SIGH-ADS scale was used to assess depression severity and the Asberg scale was used to evaluate treatment emergent side effects, defined as an increase of \u22652 from baseline measures. Correlation analyses were performed between total scale scores. The scales were compared to establish symptoms, which overlapped across scales versus symptoms, which were unique to each scale. Positive correlations were observed between the SIGH-ADS and Asberg scales and across the 8-week trial in all 3 treatment groups (correlation coefficient range 0.468-0.712). Headache was the most frequent treatment emergent side effect (10 occurrences). Fourteen symptoms were found to overlap between the 2 scales. These findings underscore the importance of reviewing somatic symptoms before administering medication to discern true treatment emergent side effects, especially in populations recovering from labor and delivery. Somatic symptoms decline in parallel with depressive symptom scores during treatment, suggesting they are indicative of underlying illness rather than side effects.\\\"}, {\\\"pmid\\\": \\\"38811474\\\", \\\"title\\\": \\\"Postpartum Depression: A Clinical Review of Impact and Current Treatment Solutions.\\\", \\\"journal\\\": \\\"Drugs\\\", \\\"year\\\": \\\"2024\\\", \\\"abstract\\\": \\\"Depression during the first year postpartum (postpartum depression) impacts millions of women and their families worldwide. In this narrative review, we provide a summary of postpartum depression, examining the etiology and consequences, pharmacological and psychological treatments, and potential mechanisms of change and current barriers to care. Psychological treatments are effective and preferred by many perinatal patients over medications, but they often remain inaccessible. Key potential mechanisms underlying their effectiveness include treatment variables (e.g., dosage and therapeutic alliance) and patient behaviors (e.g., activation and avoidance and emotional regulation). Among pharmacological treatments, the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) sertraline is generally the first-line antidepressant medication recommended to women in the postpartum period due to its minimal passage into breastmilk and the corresponding decades of safety data. Neurosteroids are emerging as an effective treatment for postpartum depression, although currently this treatment is not widely available. response.response:
- **Sample size:** 17 breastfeeding women.
- **Drugs measured:** citalopram, sertraline, and venlafaxine in maternal blood and breast milk.
- **Sertraline correlation finding:** No significant correlations were reported for sertraline. The abstract also reports lower concentration-to-dose ratios for the sertraline group than for the citalopram group.

**Long-term child developmental safety:** No. The abstract does not establish it. It reports maternal drug concentrations and estimated infant exposure, but does not report long-term child developmental outcomes. It states that more data are needed to assess effects on children’s development.

The MPRINT Gold records identify the study as:
- **Lactation — pharmacokinetics (PK)**
- **Lactation — pharmacoepidemiology (PE)**

These are classifications of the returned MPRINT records, not evidence of developmental safety. The MPRINT snapshot also cautions that it is a versioned export rather than the complete live database.

PMID 39626074 describes a **secondary analysis** of an original **8-week randomized controlled trial** involving **62 participants**. The analysis found **14 overlapping symptoms** between the depression and side-effect scales. **Headache** was the most frequent treatment-emergent side effect, with **10 occurrences**.

The original trial assessed sertraline versus transdermal estradiol and their respective placebos for major depressive disorder with postpartum onset. The MPRINT Gold record describes the study population as **Postpartum** and the study type as **CT (clinical trial)**, with a sample size of 62. MPRINT Gold did not provide the symptom-overlap or side-effect counts; those findings come from the PubMed abstract.

The abstract describes a lack of **uniform worldwide consensus about the hyperglycaemic threshold levels that qualify for a diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM)** and therefore treatment during pregnancy. It does not state a numeric threshold. [PubMed PMID 31296866](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31296866/)

- **OGTT** means **oral glucose tolerance test** and is usually used for diagnosis.
- **GCT** means **glucose challenge test** and is described as a **non-fasting screening test** used in some regions to identify women who may require a full OGTT.

The MPRINT Gold lookup returned no matching record. This reflects the limitations of the retrieved versioned MPRINT snapshot and is not evidence that no other MPRINT or broader evidence exists.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

## Comparison

| PMID | Source population | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| **35133310** | Women with epilepsy during pregnancy and reproductive care; the abstract also discusses breastfeeding | Clinical review |  
| **38841362** | **Lactation**: 37 lactating women and their infants receiving sertraline, citalopram, or paroxetine | Human **PK (pharmacokinetics)** study |

PMID 35133310 reviews pregnancy-related risks, including fetal anatomic and neurodevelopmental concerns associated with antiseizure-medication exposure. It is a review, not a medication-specific pregnancy-exposure cohort. [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35133310/)

PMID 38841362 measured drug concentrations in maternal plasma, breast milk, and infant plasma. The study reported undetectable infant plasma concentrations in all 15 infants exposed to sertraline, 9 of 13 exposed to citalopram, and 8 of 9 exposed to paroxetine. These are observed lactation pharmacokinetic findings, not pregnancy outcomes. [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38841362/)

## Can the lactation PK study alone establish fetal safety during pregnancy?

**No.** Its population was lactating women and their infants, and it assessed breast-milk transfer and infant drug exposure. It did not directly assess fetal exposure, congenital malformations, pregnancy outcomes, or fetal neurodevelopment. Therefore, it cannot by itself establish fetal safety during pregnancy.

The MPRINT Gold snapshot returned PMID 38841362 as a human lactation PK study, with the full study drug field listed as **“paroxetine, citalopram, sertraline.”** It returned no Gold record for PMID 35133310. This MPRINT snapshot is versioned and incomplete; its absence of a record is not evidence that no relevant research exists. [MPRINT Gold dataset](https://github.com/langli-lab/mprint-kp-data/blob/4bdee90dff3610816e86d0eed29b4c4d0fe76e89/gold/PK/PK_Study_cleaned_cui.csv)

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

{"response": "## Comparison

| PMID | Source population | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| **35133310** | Women with epilepsy during pregnancy and reproductive care; the abstract also discusses breastfeeding | Clinical review |

PMID 35133310 reviews pregnancy-related risks, including fetal anatomic and neurodevelopmental concerns associated with antiseizure-medication exposure. It is a review, not a medication-specific pregnancy-exposure cohort. [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35133310/)

PMID 38841362 measured drug concentrations in maternal plasma, breast milk, and infant plasma. The study reported undetectable infant plasma concentrations in all 15 infants exposed to sertraline, 9 of 13 exposed to citalopram, and 8 of 9 exposed to paroxetine. These are observed lactation pharmacokinetic findings, not pregnancy outcomes. [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38841362/)

## Can the lactation PK study alone establish fetal safety during pregnancy?

**No.** Its population was lactating women and their infants, and it assessed breast-milk transfer and infant drug exposure. It did not directly assess fetal exposure, congenital malformations, pregnancy outcomes, or fetal neurodevelopment. Therefore, it cannot by itself establish fetal safety during pregnancy.

The MPRINT Gold snapshot returned PMID 38841362 as a human lactation PK study, with the full study drug field listed as **“paroxetine, citalopram, sertraline.”** It returned no Gold record for PMID 35133310. This MPRINT snapshot is versioned and incomplete; its absence of a record is not evidence that no relevant research exists.
